clinicalPearls: Develops in patients dependent on long-term red-cell transfusion, since the body has no effective route to excrete the iron delivered by each unit
Common in thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease, myelodysplastic syndromes and other chronic transfusion-dependent anaemias
Iron accumulates first in the reticuloendothelial system and then in parenchymal organs, causing a secondary haemochromatosis
Target organs are the heart, liver and endocrine glands, producing cardiomyopathy, cirrhosis, diabetes and hypogonadism
Serum ferritin is used to monitor iron burden, and cardiac and hepatic magnetic resonance imaging quantifies tissue iron more directly
Management is iron chelation therapy, with the aim of keeping iron burden below the threshold for organ damage
Cardiac iron loading is the leading cause of death, so cardiac monitoring is central to surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Each unit of transfused red cells delivers a substantial quantity of iron, and because humans lack a regulated pathway for iron excretion, repeated transfusion inexorably expands total body iron. Once transferrin becomes saturated, non-transferrin-bound iron appears in plasma and is taken up by parenchymal cells, where it catalyses the generation of reactive oxygen species. This oxidative injury damages the myocardium, hepatocytes and endocrine tissue, leading over time to cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, and endocrine failure including diabetes and hypogonadism. Coexisting ineffective erythropoiesis in some underlying disorders suppresses hepcidin and further increases dietary iron absorption, compounding the transfusional load.
additionalDifferentials: Alcoholic or non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Other causes of dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy
Porphyria cutanea tarda with iron loading
Chronic liver disease from viral hepatitis
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin trend to estimate iron burden over time
Transferrin saturation, characteristically high in iron overload
Cardiac magnetic resonance to quantify myocardial iron
Hepatic magnetic resonance or, less commonly, biopsy to assess liver iron concentration
Liver function tests and assessment for fibrosis
Endocrine screening including glucose, thyroid and gonadal function
redFlags: New heart failure or arrhythmia suggesting cardiac iron loading
Rising ferritin despite chelation indicating inadequate iron control
Deranged liver function or signs of cirrhosis
Emerging diabetes or hypogonadism from endocrine iron deposition
reference.prognosis: With effective chelation and monitoring, organ damage can be prevented or partly reversed and survival is greatly improved, but poor adherence or late intervention leads to progressive cardiac and hepatic disease and premature death.
pitfalls: Delaying chelation until organ damage is already established
Relying on ferritin alone without imaging to assess cardiac and hepatic iron
Underestimating cardiac risk, which is the principal cause of mortality
Poor adherence to chelation going unrecognised during follow-up
